title: security: validate $match/$project field paths against allowed_models/exclude_fields
body:
## What this fixes

`_parse_match()` and `_interpret_projection()` built their field paths straight from caller input and passed them to `Q()`/`.values()` with no check against `get_published_models()` or `get_excluded_fields()`. Those two allowlists were only ever consulted for `$lookup` and for building the schema advertised to the calling model — never at query execution time.

Since the whole left-hand side of a `$match` key is caller-controlled, this also lets a Django lookup/transform be smuggled in via the field name itself (e.g. `author__password__startswith`), bypassing the `$`-operator allowlist a few lines above it.

**Net effect:** an MCP client that can query one published model can traverse any FK/M2M/reverse relation from it — including into models that were never registered with a `ModelQueryToolset` at all — and use equality/`startswith`/`regex` filters as a character-level read oracle over any field it finds, including fields explicitly listed in `exclude_fields`. Publishing a single model whose rows relate (even transitively) to `auth.User` is enough to read out password hashes one character at a time.

I reported this privately by email first; this PR accompanies that report and I'm happy to also file it as a GitHub Security Advisory once private vulnerability reporting is enabled on this repo.

## The fix

- Adds `_validate_field_path()`, mirroring the existing `_validate_lookup()`/`_resolve_model_from_path()` logic already used for `$lookup`: walk the `__`-separated path hop by hop, require each hop to be a real field, refuse a relation hop into an unpublished model, and refuse any hop that is an excluded field.
- Threaded through `_parse_match` (including its `$and`/`$or`/`$nor` recursion) and `_interpret_projection` — `$project` turned out to have the identical gap, not just `$match`.
- The no-`$project` default output path now builds its field list from the model's concrete fields minus `excluded_fields`, so `exclude_fields` actually keeps a field out of the *response*, not only out of the schema shown to the model.

## Verification

Tested against a PoC (one published `Article` model, `exclude_fields=["internal_note"]`, `auth.User` never published):

- Intended query (`{"title": "Public post"}`) is unaffected, and now correctly omits `internal_note`/`author_id` from the response body too (previously present despite `exclude_fields`).
- `{"internal_note": {"$regex": "..."}}` → `Invalid field path 'internal_note': field 'internal_note' is not available.`
- `{"author__password__startswith": "pbkdf2_sha256"}` → `Invalid field path '...': field 'author' is not available.`
- Full traversal matrix (m2m, reverse relations, unrelated apps via `auth.User`, `$regex`/`$year__gt` operators) uniformly rejected.
- `$project` on an excluded/unpublished-model field rejected the same way.
- No existing behavior for allowed fields/models changed.

## Left as suggestions, not part of this diff

- `$regex` stays available for any field that *is* published — this PR only restricts which fields/models are reachable, not lookup selection. If you'd also like to restrict `$regex` specifically (it's an efficient character-oracle and a mild ReDoS vector even on a published field), that's a separate, smaller change worth its own discussion.
- Unrelated: `pyproject.toml` pins `mcp (>=1.8.0)` with no upper bound, but current imports don't resolve against `mcp` 2.x on a fresh install — worth a version pin whenever convenient.

title: fix: use Count("pk") to support models with custom primary key (closes #65)
body:
## Summary

- Replace `Count("id")` with `Count("pk")` in the `$group` stage handler of `apply_json_mango_query` (both `$sum: 1` and `$count: 1` branches).
- Django's `pk` alias resolves to the actual primary key field regardless of its name, so this works uniformly whether the model uses the default `id` field or a custom primary key (e.g. `UUIDField(primary_key=True)`).

Closes #65.

## Test plan

- [ ] Define a model with a custom primary key (e.g. `uuid = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True)`).
- [ ] Run a pipeline containing `{"$group": {"_id": null, "total": {"$count": 1}}}` and confirm it returns a result instead of raising `FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword 'id' into field`.
- [ ] Run the same pipeline with `{"$sum": 1}` and confirm the same.
- [ ] Confirm existing models with a default `id` primary key still behave identically.

title: feat: forward icons parameter to FastMCP (closes #58)
body:
## Summary

Closes #58.

- `DjangoMCP.__init__` now accepts an optional `icons: list[Icon] | None` kwarg and forwards it to `FastMCP.__init__`, so MCP clients (e.g. Claude Desktop) can display a server icon next to the server name.
- The option is also usable via `DJANGO_MCP_GLOBAL_SERVER_CONFIG`:
  ```python
  from mcp.types import Icon

  DJANGO_MCP_GLOBAL_SERVER_CONFIG = {
      "name": "mymcp",
      "icons": [
          Icon(src="https://example.com/icon.png", mimeType="image/png", sizes=["64x64"]),
      ],
  }
  ```
- The `icons` keyword was introduced in `mcp` **1.15.0** ([SEP 973](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/pull/1357)), so the lower bound on the `mcp` dependency is bumped from `1.8.0` to `1.15.0`. Latest `mcp` today is `1.27.0`, so this is a conservative floor.
- README updated: new bullet under the `DJANGO_MCP_GLOBAL_SERVER_CONFIG` settings reference and an example in the "Customize the default MCP server settings" section.

No change to existing behavior when `icons` is omitted (default `None` is accepted by `FastMCP`).

## Test plan

- [x] New `DjangoMCPIconsTest` in `examples/mcpexample/bird_counter/tests.py`:
  - `test_icons_default_is_none` — constructing without `icons` keeps `_mcp_server.icons` as `None`.
  - `test_icons_forwarded_to_fastmcp` — passing `icons=[...]` propagates the list to the underlying `MCPServer`.
- [x] `pytest` in `examples/mcpexample/` — all 10 tests pass (8 existing + 2 new).
- [x] `python manage.py check` on the example project — clean.

title: Enforce ModelQueryToolset.fields as a real output boundary
body:
## Problem

`ModelQueryToolset.fields` is documented as "the list of fields to include" and is used to render the LLM-facing schema — but it is not enforced anywhere on the query path. The final step of `apply_json_mango_query` calls `queryset.values()` with no arguments, returning every concrete column on the model. As a result:

1. **Undeclared fields leak in output.** Any column an authenticated caller can see on a visible row — including columns the toolset author deliberately omitted from `fields` — is reachable by simply omitting `$project`, by projecting directly (`{"$project": {"street": 1}}`), or by renaming (`{"$project": {"renamed": "$street"}}`).
2. **Non-serializable columns crash the renderer.** When an undeclared column is non-JSON-serializable (common example: GeoDjango `PointField`), the default `.values()` hands it to the DRF JSON renderer and the whole tool call raises `TypeError: Object of type Point is not JSON serializable`.

## Change

Treat `fields` as a real output boundary when it is declared. Two silent-strip points:

- **No `$project`**: the default `.values()` is restricted to `allowed_fields` (declared `fields` minus `get_excluded_fields()`) instead of every concrete column.
- **Explicit `$project`**: mappings whose source field is undeclared are dropped from the spec before interpretation. Covers both direct (`{"street": 1}`) and rename-bypass (`{"renamed": "$street"}`) forms. Alias-prefixed sources (`$loc.name`) and exclusions (`{"_id": 0}`) pass through unchanged.

Wiring: `apply_json_mango_query` gains an optional `allowed_fields` parameter. `_QueryExecutor.query` derives it from the toolset via a small `_allowed_fields_for()` helper.

## Backwards compatibility

Additive. Toolsets that don't declare `fields` (`fields = None`) get the previous unrestricted behaviour — every column returned, no filtering. Nothing changes for existing code until the author opts in by declaring `fields`.

## Out of scope

`$match` / `$sort` on undeclared columns still execute at the DB layer. That leaves a "does this row exist" side-channel but no value leak in output. Closing the side-channel needs pipeline-reference validation and is deferred.

## Tests

`UndeclaredFieldsNotReturnedTest` in `examples/mcpexample/bird_counter/tests.py` pins the guarantee across all three paths:

- `test_undeclared_fields_are_not_returned` — no-`$project` default
- `test_explicit_project_to_declared_field_works` — legitimate `$project` still works
- `test_project_to_undeclared_field_is_silently_stripped` — direct leak closed
- `test_project_renamed_from_undeclared_field_is_silently_stripped` — rename bypass closed
- `test_no_allowed_fields_preserves_legacy_behaviour` — backwards compatibility

Full suite (13 tests, 8 original + 5 new) passes.

title: feat: add register_drf_filter_tool for django-filter integration
body:
## Summary

Adds `register_drf_filter_tool` and `drf_publish_filter_mcp_tool` — a new DRF tool registration method that automatically exposes `django-filter` FilterSet parameters as typed, optional MCP tool inputs.

This is the feature proposed in #62.

### What it does

When a DRF `ListModelMixin` ViewSet has a `filterset_class` or `filterset_fields`, `register_drf_filter_tool` reads every declared filter and registers it as a typed tool parameter (bool, float, or str). A `limit` parameter caps the result set. Agents see a fully documented schema — updating a FilterSet automatically updates the tool's interface.

### Example usage

**Imperative:**
```python
from mcp_server import mcp_server

mcp_server.register_drf_filter_tool(
    CampaignViewSet,
    actions={'get': 'list'},
    instructions="Search campaigns by any filter field.",
)
```

**Decorator:**
```python
from mcp_server import drf_publish_filter_mcp_tool

@drf_publish_filter_mcp_tool(actions={'get': 'list'})
class CampaignViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    filterset_class = CampaignFilter
    ...
```

### Design decisions

- **Separate module** (`mcp_server/drf_filter.py`): All `django-filter`-specific logic (helpers, `_DRFFilterCallerTool`, `register_drf_filter_tool`) lives here, keeping the optional dependency boundary clean.
- **Thin delegates in `djangomcp.py`**: `DjangoMCP.register_drf_filter_tool()` method and `drf_publish_filter_mcp_tool` decorator follow the existing pattern (like `register_drf_list_tool` / `drf_publish_list_mcp_tool`) and delegate to the new module via a lazy import.
- **`django-filter` is optional**: An `ImportError` with a helpful message is raised only when `register_drf_filter_tool` is actually called without `django-filter` installed. No impact on users who don't use this feature.
- **Dynamic `inspect.Signature`**: The async wrapper gets a proper signature so that `func_metadata` builds the correct Pydantic `arg_model`, ensuring arguments are validated and forwarded correctly.

### Files changed

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `mcp_server/drf_filter.py` | **New** — 190 lines: helpers, caller class, registration function |
| `mcp_server/djangomcp.py` | +68 lines: thin method + decorator |
| `mcp_server/__init__.py` | +1 export: `drf_publish_filter_mcp_tool` |

### Testing

- Existing test suite passes (8/8 in `examples/mcpexample`).
- Battle-tested in production against 18 DRF ViewSets with complex FilterSets.

Closes #62

title: feat: add DJANGO_MCP_SERVER_CLASS setting to allow custom DjangoMCP subclass
body:
## Problem
`global_mcp_server` is hardcoded to use `DjangoMCP`, making it impossible 
to use a custom subclass without monkey-patching the module.

This is a common need when users want to override methods like 
`register_drf_list_tool` to add custom behavior (e.g. extra params, 
custom serialization, pagination support).

## Solution
Add a `DJANGO_MCP_SERVER_CLASS` setting following Django's `import_string` 
pattern, allowing users to provide their own `DjangoMCP` subclass.

## Usage
```python
# settings.py
DJANGO_MCP_SERVER_CLASS = 'myapp.mcp.MyCustomDjangoMCP'
```

## Notes
- Fully backwards compatible — defaults to `DjangoMCP` if not set
- Validates that the custom class is a subclass of `DjangoMCP` and raises 
  `ImproperlyConfigured` if not
- Follows Django's existing conventions (`import_string`, `ImproperlyConfigured`)

title: Fix DRF Integration Body Processing and API Failure Issues
body: ## Summary This PR fixes critical bugs in the Django REST Framework integration and adopts a cleaner architectural approach using composition over method patching. ## Bugs Fixed ### 1. **Body Parameter Mapping Issue** - **Github Issue Link:** Closes https://github.com/omarbenhamid/django-mcp-server/issues/39 - **Problem**: MCP tool calls made with data nested inside a body property (e.g., `{"body": {"title": "...", "content": "..."}}`) were not being properly extracted for DRF serializers - **Symptom**: DRF validation errors showing required fields as missing, even though they were present in the MCP call - **Root Cause**: The request initialization flow was returning the original MCP JSON-RPC request instead of the fabricated request containing the extracted body data - **Fix**: Proper data flow from MCP body parameters to DRF serializer data ### 2. **Global ViewSet Patching Breaking Normal HTTP Requests** - **Github Issue Link:** Closes https://github.com/omarbenhamid/django-mcp-server/issues/32 - **Problem**: The `initialize_request` method was being globally patched on ViewSet classes, affecting ALL requests to those ViewSets, including normal API requests - **Symptom**: Normal HTTP API requests (e.g., `curl localhost:8000/posts/`) failed with `AttributeError: 'WSGIRequest' object has no attribute 'original_request'` - **Root Cause**: Method patching modified the class permanently, expecting MCP-specific request attributes on normal Django requests - **Fix**: MCP requests conform to the same interface expectations as normal API requests and patching has been removed all together ## Technical Strategy Instead of trying to bypass or hack DRF's request creation, we pre-process the MCP request into exactly what DRF expects (a simple Django HttpRequest) and then let DRF run its full lifecycle using its intended mechanisms. The benefits of this approach are: 1. Let DRF's unmodified initialize_request do its job naturally 2. DRF creates a proper rest_framework.request.Request with all the bells and whistles 3. Full DRF lifecycle runs: parsers, authentication, permissions, etc. The potential drawbacks are: 1. We are using a Factory from DRF's testing library, which is probably not intended to be used for runtime purposes. In future version of DRF this may break (as the factory is likely to be extended to suit new testing needs). ## Demo / Testing Here are screenshots of my really simple Blog Post app (see code [here](https://github.com/omarbenhamid/django-mcp-server/issues/39)) working with Claude Desktop: Here's my really simple Blog Post app normal API calls working: All tests in the bird_counter example app pass:

title: Add Claude local memory files to .gitignore
body:
This is a housekeeping change that improves the developer experience when using Claude Code with this repository.

**Changes**

- Added CLAUDE.local.md pattern to .gitignore

**Rationale**

When using Claude Code to write code in django-mcp-server, I might want to tell Claude to "remember" things related to what we're working on. Claude puts this info in `CLAUDE.local.md` by adding these files to `.gitignore`, we ensure that developers can use Claude Code's memory features without cluttering the repository. Note that `CLAUDE.md` is NOT ignored so that if one day we want to start creating and committing shared Claude documentation, we can.
